body: This seems too specific to me. I agree that we should rephrase this paragraph to make it clearer what this parameter does. But I'm not sure we should focus specifically on the root node case.

I do see what you mean about it being too specific, but I think it's important to specify root because it's a unique and useful case. Perhaps we can rephrase it as such?

"If owned is true, only descendants with a valid owner node are checked. This would exclude `SceneTree.root`, orphans without parents, and new children whose `owner` was never set."

body:
This method and `find_children` are somewhat of a design mistake that may be addressed next time we can.
There's no reason why `owned` should be set to `true` by default, nor why it's finding children owned by _any_ node. Both aspects make this method very misleading.

With that said I don't think this information should be here. The big clarification following the parameter's description is one good way to overwhelm the reader with redundant and specific information.
At most, the tip in this PR should be a new note at the bottom of the description.

Keep in mind that the reader can naturally come to this same conclusion by acknowledging that the `root` node is not owned by any other node. This tidbit could also be lightly mentioned in `root` itself.

body:
I am a game developer using Godot as my engine for two concurrent projects I plan to release. Implicit implementation details should not be required to know when reading basic node documentation. This wasted a bit of my own time as well.

While the fact that the root node is not owned by other nodes makes sense, but I don't understand why it needs to be owned just to find its children. The functions "find_child()" and "find_children()" imply that any existing node that has children, should be able to return the value of one of or multiple of their children, regardless of whether this node has other parents of its own. 

This fact makes less sense to me when considering that "get_child()" and "get_children()" work from the root node. 

If the SceneTree.root use case was explicitely added to the documentation, or even better, a warning given in the engine itself when this use case is written, that would go a long way in assisting developers. This would not be overwhelming or redundant in this case, as it would directly tackle the issue that was causing my (and I assume @RolandMarchand's) time to be wasted. To me, personally, however, I can't say I follow the logic that a node that isn't "owned" can't find its own children. This seems like an implementation detail.
